utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Case IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning. If Your Honours please, my name is Di Fazio and I appear for the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, appearing for Mr. Naser Oric. Joining us here today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts. Your Honours, we are not receiving any interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not good news, since for this sitting we will be relying mostly on the technical expertise and facilities that we have. I have been saying something in English precisely so that -- can you receive interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Now I can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So are there any preliminary matters that you'd like to raise before we start -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm having a little bit of trouble myself with my headphones, if Your Honours please. I can't get any reception through them. I hope I'm not doing something obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can change them for you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Ah, then I'm ready to go, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter I might mention while the technical difficulty is being dealt with. As I indicated to my learned friend, we would need approximately an hour and a half with this witness. I know yesterday Your Honour expressed a desire to be finished with this witness today. So from the planning point of view, if I were to start my cross-examination at approximately 11.30 today, then that wouldn't present any difficulties. If it were much after that, then we might run into difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, hers is a very simple story, and I'm hopeful that I can finish it in the time. I'll do everything possible. I'm confident that I'll be able to finish by about 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I thought we would be finished with this witness in chief and cross by 10.30. Because it's such a simply story and straightforward, I simply can't understand or figure this happening in a national jurisdiction. A witness like this would last maximum half an hour, maximum. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it is a very simple story, if Your Honours please. There are a number of details that we have to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm aware of what you want, and I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just stick to the events that are relevant to the indictment and avoid asking the witness questions that relate to events that are not part of the indictment, unless they were relevant for the purpose of the indictment. Mr. Siller in Belgrade, can you hear me and can you see me? Yes, I can see you but I cannot hear you. In the background, yes. In the background, yes. But I get the impression that I'm hearing you because there is another microphone nearby, not through your own microphone. Could you repeat? We've just raised the volume a little bit. Yes, could I ask you to repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Your Honours, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Now I can hear you more than I should, actually. Okay, thank you. So is the witness, Svetlana Trifunovic near you, Mr. Siller?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Yes. The witness is sitting into the room next to us here, and if you want me to bring the witness in, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any matters that you wish to raise in relation to this witness before we bring her in the room where she will be testifying? MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, none. Yes, Mr. Siller. You can admit the witness into the room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And before you do so, has she been briefed? Would someone brief her as to the procedure? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I certainly did as to the general procedure that would be adopted, if Your Honours please, when I proofed her. I think she knows what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the important thing, because this could frighten her if she is not used to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] I can tell you that the witness has been brought in and she knows what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Siller. And do you have handy the text of the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Yes. I have it handy. It's here on my desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm going to address the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Your Honours, the witness can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure, madam, that you can follow what I am saying in English in your own language, in other words, that you are receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did he say? Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Trifunovic, would you please look at the camera and listen to what I have to tell you. I am the Presiding Judge. At the moment, I am presiding over the case against Naser Oric here at -- the time of 9.20 almost in The Hague, in the Netherlands. You are one of the witnesses for the Prosecution, and we have granted permission to have your testimony given via videolink. I wish to inform you that very soon your testimony will start, but before we start with your testimony, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration, which is equivalent to an oath, is contained in a piece of paper which my man over there, Mr. Siller, will be handing to you. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us, that in the course of your testimony, you will be testifying the truth. Could you follow what I was staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- MR. DI FAZIO: I can hear what she is saying, but I'm not getting Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond any translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither could I. Let's go through it again. Ms. Trifunovic, could I ask you to read out that solemn declaration again, please, because it did not get through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Trifunovic. I ask for your indulgence and your patience, should things not work out 100 per cent. This is modern technology and sometimes we encounter glitches. So please, if it doesn't work 100 per cent, I ask you to bear with us a little bit and be patient. I am now going to ask Mr. Di Fazio, who you have met before, who is one of the officers of the Prosecution in this case, he is going to ask you a series of questions. After, when he's finished, you will be asked a series of questions on cross-examination by Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Naser Oric. Your responsibility as a witness is to answer all questions, irrespective of who is putting them to you, to answer all questions truly and fully, in accordance with the solemn declaration that you have made. Please try to be concise in your answers, to the point, and don't say things that you are not asked about. In other words, restrict your answer to the question, and please don't try to go beyond that. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ms. Trifunovic, in addition to what His Honour just told you, if you answer the question with a yes or no, that would help me. So just remember that, please. If you can just say yes or no, that's of considerable use. You were born in 1981, and in January of 1993, I think you were about 11 years old; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you're of Serb ethnicity, and in 1993, you were living in a small village --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In 1993, you were living in a small village called Kostolomci; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And you lived there with your mother, I believe, your grandfather and your grandmother; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just need the names of your mother and your grandfather. What are they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Zivana and Mile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to direction your attention to events that occurred in 1993, in January of 1993, events that occurred between the Serb Christmas that year and the New Year. Do you remember, first of all, that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Around that period of time, or, I should say, between those two festivals, Christmas and New Year, was your village attacked?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: During the course of the attack, was your mother captured?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the ethnicity of the soldiers who attacked your village of Kostolomci.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What makes you say that? Why do you say to the Trial Chamber that they were Muslim soldiers? Was there anything that you heard them saying, or is it the way they spoke, something about the way they dressed, anything at all that you can think of that makes you say that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: By their clothes and by their voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you remember how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Green, green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they have any insignia or any attachments to their green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They had black ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were they tied?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Around their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were 12, I think. Once the attack started and you saw your mother captured --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Bit of stage fright there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Once the attack started and your mother was captured, did you flee, did you run away?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where did you run?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We ran straight away, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm asking about you. Where did you, you in particular, you the little girl, aged 12, run? Where did you run to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: To the bakery, my uncle's bakery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at your uncle's bakery?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: One night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you alone there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you return to your house?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, in the morning, I returned to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your house empty?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were all the possessions that had formally been in your house, all the household goods and so on, were they still there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: During that day, did you see anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim soldiers when you returned to your house?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: At around 11.00, Muslim soldiers arrived and they took me prisoner in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they come into your house and capture you there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Again, how were these soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In green uniforms, with black bands around their arms, black armbands, and their faces were painted black.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did these soldiers take you away?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They took me to a village called Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you were being taken from Kostolomci, having been captured, did you see any other soldiers, apart from the men who captured you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What were they doing? The other soldiers, what were they doing in Kostolomci as you were being taken away? What were they up to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were looting and killing Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They killed all the Serb soldiers, and then they looted and captured people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there Serb soldiers in Kostolomci?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were some, but they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When were they killed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Before I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were these Serb soldiers men who had been living in the village of Kostolomci?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Local villagers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Now, you said that you were taken to Jagodnja. Were you the only prisoner of the soldiers who took you there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: My mother and my grandfather were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But you were taken, weren't you, from Kostolomci to Jagodnja. During that particular trip, were you alone with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, where were you taken to in Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: To a cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your mother and your grandfather there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from the day you fled Kostolomci and went to hide in the bakery, did you ever see your grandmother again?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in the cellar in Jagodnja with your grandfather and your mother, how was your grandfather dressed; can you recall?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't wearing a uniform, he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber about how old he was back then, back then in 1993. If you don't know precisely, can you tell us if he was an old man or whether he was still in his 50s or ... Can you give us some idea of how old he was?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was an old man, but I don't know how old he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you ever seen your grandfather walking around Kostolomci with a gun, guarding the village?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He never carried a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Was your grandfather in the army, in the VRS or the JNA, just prior to these events that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He had done his army service, but he wasn't in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. He had done his army service as a young man, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived in Jagodnja and you saw your mother and your grandfather, did they appear -- did they show any signs of any beating?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They told me they had been beaten, but I didn't see any signs on them. I was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. How long did you stay in Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: One night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The next day, were you, your grandfather, and your mother taken to a place called Osmace?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And were you, again, the only prisoners being escorted to Osmace?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you or your mother or your grandfather on the way from Jagodnja to Osmace, if you can remember anything?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: When we were going from Jagodnja to Osmace, nothing happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And, again, what was the ethnicity of the soldiers who escorted you from Jagodnja to Osmace?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are assuming and you are asking the witness to assume or agree with you that they were soldiers. You did not put the question whether they were soldiers in the first place. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, Your Honour is quite right. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who are the people who took you from Jagodnja and Osmace?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they dressed in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were dressed in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they have the black ribbons that you have spoken of? Were they wearing them?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived in Osmace, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: To the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were you kept there overnight, along with your mother and grandfather?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The next day, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, we were taken to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did it take you to make your way from Osmace to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many kilometres it is. I'd never even heard of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did anything happen to you, your grandfather or your mother on the way from Osmace to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They found a knife --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who found a knife?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- the Muslim soldiers did. The Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what happened with the knife?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They took it and, on the knife, there was a name written. It was "koljac," the throat-cutter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was done with the knife?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They threatened us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was it who accompanied you from Osmace to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm not quite sure whether it's my fault or not, but the witness, when referring to the knife, I recollect hearing her say "they found a knife," but I don't recollect her saying exactly where they found the knife, whether it was on the person of one of them or whether it was just in the truck or lorry or whatever. I think it's relevant to know. Because if it was found just lying on the truck, is one thing; if it was found on the person of one of them, it's another. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. I understand where Your Honour is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let's just go back to the knife. You told us about a knife being found on the way from Osmace to Srebrenica. Where was the knife located when it was found?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So it was found lying on the road by one of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thinking back, can you tell the Trial Chamber if either you, your mother or your grandfather were armed in any way, at any time from the point of your capture up until the time you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just the soldiers that you have said accompanied you and who were dressed in green uniforms, were they also sporting the black ribbons?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You may or may not remember this. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if the two soldiers who originally captured you escorted you from Jagodnja to Osmace, and from Osmace to Srebrenica. Were they in the group of escorting soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were among the group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to your arrival in Srebrenica. Had you ever been to Srebrenica before? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: To the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say "the prisons." What sort of building was it that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was a low and long building. It was all on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did it appear to be the house -- private house of a person, or did it appear to you to be some sort of public building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It looked like a detention place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Were you taken to a room in that building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: To a room where the other prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you remain in custody for the next month until your exchange?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to get some details for the Trial Chamber of that month that you spent in custody in Srebrenica. Firstly, were the women prisoners all kept in one cell?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you kept in there with them?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you aware of any male prisoners in the building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the same building but in a different room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Was the room that the male prisoners were kept in close to the room where the female prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We weren't in the same room. The men were in one room and we women were in another room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a lavatory nearby, close to both rooms where the male prisoners were kept and the female prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you taken there from time to time, to the lavatory, by the guards?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see where the door to the male prisoners' cell was as you were taken from your room to the lavatory?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far was the male prisoners' door from the female prisoners' door? What distance, approximately, if you can't tell us exactly?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. On the occasions that you were taken to the lavatory, were you able to see if guards had their own room?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And about how far away from your women's cell was the guards' room located?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Also about two or three steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned the presence of guards in the prison. What ethnicity were those guards?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see them armed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What colour uniform?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Green.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you -- thinking back, can you recall any other feature or insignia of their uniform, other than the fact that it was green?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They had black ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Like the ribbons of the soldiers who captured you in Kostolomci and escorted you back to Srebrenica, the same sort of black ribbons, or were they different?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They had black ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now let's focus on the women's cell where you were kept. About how many women were in there in custody with you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: About 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you the youngest?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your mother in custody there with you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you first arrived at the prison completing your walk from Osmace, was your grandfather still with you, still a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he placed in custody in the cell belonging to the men?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were any of the women in custody with you wounded?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were the women in custody with you, were they all women of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't need individual descriptions, but can you tell the Trial Chamber what sort of women they were. Did they appear to be local peasant women? Did they appear to be women from the town? Did they appear to be soldiers? Can you comment on what sort of women they were?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: These were local women.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What ages did they range from? Were they all young? Were some of them young, were some of them middle-aged, were some of them old; or was it a combination of all three age groups?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them were younger and some were middle-aged and some were elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to give the Trial Chamber a picture of the conditions inside the women's cell. Firstly, it was January 1993. Was it cold?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was warm because we had heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what sort of heating did you have? Tell the Trial Chamber of the heating facilities that were given to you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There was a stove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how was the stove used? Was it used with firewood?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with firewood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who brought the firewood, and how often?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, they would bring in two sacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: All day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many blankets did you have?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: About four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You had four blankets?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You personally had four blankets?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not me personally. All of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Four blankets for about 20 women; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were four blankets in that room. There was a bench, and the blankets were on the bench. We were not issued with blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where did you sleep at night?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have anything underneath you, any blankets on top of you? What was the bedding like? Did you understand my question? I asked you about the bedding when you slept at night. Did you have blankets, mattresses, pillows? Describe to the Trial Chamber so that they understand and know what the bedding was like at nights for you women.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it warm at night?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any bedding at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it warm at night?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the month that you were in custody, were you able to wash?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was it customary for the women to be escorted from the women's cell to the lavatory about once a day?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They let us go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now let's -- I want to ask you about the men's cell. Did you ever go into the men's cell, as far as you can remember? Did you ever go inside it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Ilija Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Srebrenica during that month that you were in custody?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: When I was going to the toilet, that's when I saw him. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you know Ilija Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Because he was from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you scared at all during that month that you were in custody?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the guards ever come into your women's cell?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you feel when that happened?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Terrible. I was frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How would you react when they came into the women's cell?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the guards ever mistreat the women in the sense of beating them physically?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't beat them, but they threatened them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of threats were directed towards the women in the cell?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They said that they would kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What would you do when these threats were being uttered?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's return to the men's cell. Apart from Ilija Ivanovic, did you see any of the other men who were in the men's cell on your way to the lavatory, when you were taken to the lavatory? Or was he the only one that you can recall seeing?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: My grandfather was there too, and I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you saw Ivanovic and your grandfather, did they have any marks on them, any marks on their face?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What could you see --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This person was wounded, you could see a mark on his face. And my grandfather was black and blue all over his face. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From your position inside the women's cell, could you hear voices from the men's cell?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: When they cried.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How often could you hear the men crying?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you say they cried, do you mean that you could hear them sobbing in the sense of tears, or do you mean in the sense of crying out in pain, or perhaps both?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: When they were being beaten, they were crying out in pain, because they were suffering pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When they were being beaten, could you hear any other noise, apart from the -- apart from human voices, at the same time that they were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could hear the Muslim soldiers laughing, and the Serbs who were in the cell were crying and moaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: You've told the Trial Chamber that you never went into the men's cell, so you don't know -- you couldn't see what was happening in there.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if the Serb -- if the Muslim guards took in objects, anything at all, sticks or guns or anything, into the men's cell? Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Bats or sticks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me return to that question I asked you a moment ago. Did you hear anything during the course of these beatings, other than human voices, other than cries of pain, other than the utterances of the Muslim guards? Did you hear anything else? Let me rephrase the question. Could you hear --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Could you hear bats being used?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know what that means, could you hear a bat being used. My learned friend has already put -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that you heard sounds --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I heard shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From the cell -- from the men's cell?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How often did you hear that, or was it only on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now you've told us how often sounds of beatings were heard, every three hours. On how many days in that month that you were kept in custody did you hear the sounds of beatings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, I know, every three hours. But was that every three hours once a week, was it every day of every week? That's what I want to know. How often during the month.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you hear your grandfather's voice during the course of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you hear him crying out?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How often would you hear him crying out? Was it only on one or two occasions? Was it more often?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: More often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time that you were in custody, did you hear the name Naser Oric mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's completely an inappropriate question. Really, my learned friend should asked what she heard, if she heard names. She shouldn't put the name of this accused in this trial. It's a clear suggestion that this witness should remember that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see how your objection can be sustained. She is being asked whether a particular name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He could ask whether she heard any names, first of all, and if she says no, then it would be clear that she hadn't heard the name Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would be, perhaps, more correct. But let's proceed that way, Mr. Di Fazio. You first ask her whether any names were mentioned. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you hear any names mentioned in the month that you were in custody?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were mentioning the name of this man called Oric, saying that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you say they were mentioning this. Who mentioned it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Two Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember in any more detail what they said? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: When I was to be exchanged, that's when they said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So it was towards the end of your stay in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And tell the Trial Chamber what was said to you, and how the name Oric came up.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: My mother and I were being taken to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what can you recall being said about Oric?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to your exchange. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one more question on that. The person who said that Oric was in charge, who was that? I don't mean their identity. But was it a guard or someone else?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Those were other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was this said on your way from the women's cell to some other place?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that while I was in the cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More important, Mr. Di Fazio, is the context in which this person, whoever it was, would mention the person who is in charge, and precisely also by name. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, were you eventually exchanged, you and your mother?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the Jadar, that's where we were exchanged, the two of us only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other women prisoners remained in the cell, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you taken -- who took you from the women's cell on the day that you were exchanged, or the day that the process of exchange started?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim soldiers entered our cell and took us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Took you where?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They took us on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: To where?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: To a village called Vizjatra.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, after you were taken from the cell and before you were put on the truck, were you taken anywhere? Or was it the case that you were simply taken from your cell and put on a truck?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They took us to a village and we spent a night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now let's cast your mind back to the period of time on that day when the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I hate doing this, but I have been asked to give the witness a break, so instead of having the break at 10.30, we'll have the break now, if you don't mind. I'm sorry to interrupt you so abruptly. MR. DI FAZIO: It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not something I like doing, but I think we need to do that straight away. MR. DI FAZIO: I can also indicate that I'm getting close to the end, so it's working out quite well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But Madam Trifunovic needs a short break. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a break of 30 minutes, all right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Trifunovic, any time you need us to stop and give you a break, a rest, please let me know. Could you follow what I was saying? Were you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed, and conclude. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. It won't be long now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ms.. Trifunovic, I was asking you about the occasion when you were being taken from the women's cell and being taken off for the process of exchange. You've already told us that a guard came and took you from the cell and that you were put on a truck. Now, during that time when the guard came and the time when you were put on the truck, is that when you heard the name Oric mentioned, or was it on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the name mentioned when I was in detention. That's when I heard his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you recall who mentioned his name?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you only heard it once or it was on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember what was said?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Something to do with the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So you heard his name mentioned while you were in custody, and it was in the context of your exchange; do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to finish up on this topic, there's nothing else that you can recall about what was said when Mr. Oric's name was mentioned, or do you just remember the fact that it was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's the only thing I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We'll leave this topic and we'll move on to your exchange. Was your mother entrusted with taking a note to Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, did she, in fact, do that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who entrusted her with the note to take to the Serb soldiers? Who gave it to her?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And did she leave you for a while in Jadar and go off on her mission with the note?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was that day, and she took the message across while I remained with the Muslim soldiers at Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did she return to you that day, or was it the next day?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The same day. She left in the morning and came back in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Both you and your mother?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who were you exchanged for; can you recall?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were exchanged, the two of us who were still alive, and we were exchanged for three bodies of Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From the point of time that you were captured until you were exchanged, in that month period of time, did anyone other than Muslim soldiers guard you, issue instructions to you, tell you what to do?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your grandfather eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a place called Uzice Hospital?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your grandfather ever taken to Uzice Hospital?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not before he was captured. It was after he was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did he find his way to Uzice Hospital?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was exchanged at a later stage. He got sick and an ambulance took him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. Your grandfather underwent the same -- similar exchange process that you and your mother underwent, and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond then he was taken to hospital; is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- about how long after your exchange that your grandfather was exchanged? It doesn't have to be exact.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see him in Uzice Hospital, or indeed, did you see him at any time --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- after the exchange?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, about twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did he look when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was emaciated and all black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he eventually die?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how long after his exchange did he die?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was exchanged several days later. He lived on for a couple of days and then he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the fate of your grandmother?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Trifunovic. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Madam Trifunovic, I'm now going to pass you on to Mr. Jones, who is defending Mr. Oric in this trial. He will be asking you a series of questions. Thank you. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Trifunovic, this morning my learned friend suggested to you on a couple of occasions that you were 12 at the time of your capture. It's right, isn't it, that you were actually 11, 11 and a half at that time? You were born in July 1981; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So 11. And you're now --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- a mother -- you're now a mother with two children, I believe. These events took place a long time ago, and I imagine they seemed -- my apologies, I'll slow down. They must seem a distant memory to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, over the last 11, nearly 12 years since these events, I take it you've spoken to people about these events, in particular your mother who went to Srebrenica with you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And with other people, I imagine, as well; for example, your husband.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were from -- at the time you were living in Kostolomci. That's near Skelani, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Have you since been told or learnt that you were captured on the 16th of January, 1993? Because you weren't sure about the date before.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want you to bear in mind when I ask you some questions today that you're to tell us what you yourself remember, difficult though that may be given the distance of time, and not tell us what other people have told you about events, but what you saw as an 11-year-old girl back then. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, a couple of questions relating to Kostolomci. You mentioned going to a bakery when you ran away, belonging to your uncle. Was his name Drago?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you last saw your grandmother when you ran from your house. Is it right that you last saw her when you were by Milenko's house, Milenko being a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw her as I was running away. Near Milenko's stable, we parted ways, and we never saw each other again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told us that on the way to Srebrenica and subsequently in the prison that threats were made to you and to others. It's right to say, isn't it, that those threats were never carried out; they remained just words.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you arrived in Srebrenica, you came by foot, I take it, from Osmace.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As you came into the town, did you see thousands of Muslim civilians living out on the streets in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall the conditions under which they were living, namely, having fires outside, living on the streets? Is that something you recall?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall their appearing to be in a pretty bad state, those people you saw in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you spent one month in the prison, in the same room with about 20 women. So is it right that that would have been from one or two days after the 16th of January --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and so you would have stayed there until around the 18th or 19th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the names of some, at least, of the women who you spent that month with?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I only know that one of those women was called Milena.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall a Milenija Mitrovic? Was she there with you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So apart from Milenija and Milena, can you tell us the names of any of the other 18 or so women who you say you spent one month with?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, try, if you may. Can you not remember any other names of any of those other women?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about them, about what they were wearing or where they were from?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: From Bosnia, from the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's all you remember of those women?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember a little Serb boy called Branko who came to the prison with a lady cook who brought the food?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember a woman called Behara with whom you stayed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that once you arrived in Srebrenica, nobody touched a hair on your head or that of your mother or any of the women. None of them were physically mistreated in any way.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You had a stove in your cell for warmth, and you were given food every day, I think it's correct to say, bread and beans. It's right, isn't it, also, that you each had a blanket.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you referred to men being beaten in the prison, and you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me interrupt you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Trifunovic, can you explain to me how you can state now that each one of you had a blanket when previously you said that there were only four blankets there for all of you? I mean, I can't tie up the two statements together, because they seem to be contradictory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were thirsty. Four blankets in that room, and the 20 of us had to share those four blankets. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall making a statement in July 2000 to investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You may not have it in front of you. A copy may be provided. But for the moment, I'm looking at 02 -- ERN 02170348 of the English version, page 5 of 8, paragraph 3, which says: "We each had one blanket." So you're saying that's not correct, it's not true that you each had one blanket?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you heard beatings of the men in the prison every three hours, and you were very clear and deliberate about that. You said that it was every three hours for the month --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- you were imprisoned. Did you have a watch at this time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So not having a watch, an 11-year-old girl in these conditions, which you describe as frightening, how can you be so categorical that on the dot, every three hours, men were being beaten for this period of one month? How did you be so sure?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Because this is something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you're absolutely sure that every three hours exactly you heard these beatings --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and that that went on for one month. That's your evidence.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you've mentioned seeing that your grandfather was black and blue. It's right, isn't it, that he was beaten before he was brought to the prison in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also mentioned Ilija Ivanovic, who you said you knew as he was from your village. He's, in fact, from Kosici, isn't he, rather than from your village?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit further along the road, but it's still part of the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You didn't yourself actually see anyone being beaten, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I heard them being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you don't know who beat them, whether they were men, women, civilians, soldiers, Serbs, Muslims --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, you didn't see that, though, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim soldiers, that's who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it your evidence that you slept at the prison every night of your captivity, from the 18th of January until the 18th of February?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then you've told us you were exchanged. You said in your statement given to the investigators of this Tribunal that your house was destroyed during the attack of 16th January 1993. I'm looking at the ERN 02170349: "Our house was completely destroyed during the attack." That's not true, is it, because you went back the next day?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was destroyed. Everything was destroyed, with the exception of one room.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But when you went back on the next day after you had run away, you said how you went there and there were -- I think you said that -- let me put it a different way. You went back to the house and entered it, and it hadn't been destroyed on that occasion at all.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everything had been destroyed, with the exception of one room.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us today that shortly before you were exchanged you were told that someone called Oric was in charge. Am I right in understanding that to mean that he was in charge of the exchange which was about to take place, that that's how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that I heard in Srebrenica prior to the exchange, from other soldiers who said that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In charge of the exchange. All right. And at the time the name Oric didn't mean anything to you at all, did it? There's no particular reason why it would have stuck in your mind. Sorry, did you understand my question? We seem to have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During video-conferencing, this happens. So just wait. Eventually she'll get the question. Could you please repeat the question to make sure she does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you heard the name Oric, that's not a name which meant anything to you at all, did it? It was not a name that you had heard before for which there was any reason why it should stick in your mind.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it did stick in my mind for some reason. It's something I heard prior to the exchange, and I still remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you saw the guards in the prison, I imagine, every day. Do you remember the names of any of those guards?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the cooks who prepared the food for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And apart from the few detainees who you mentioned, do you remember the names of any of the other people who you encountered when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember a one-armed man called Zele?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So just so we're absolutely clear, you spent a month with 20-odd women; there were cooks, guards, and other people. You remember practically none of those names, but you say that you do remember the name Oric, from 12 years ago, 11, 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just heard that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The fact is, isn't it, that the name Oric has been something -- is a name you've been told since you were released by Serbs, and you've been told to mention that name in relation to your detention, and that you didn't hear the name at the time.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I hadn't heard his name before I was detained, but I heard it while I was in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to refer you to your statement from 2000 to the investigators, and it's not necessarily to put a copy in front of you for the moment. But just for the record, it's ERN 02170345, second paragraph. And there you say: "In 1993, I was interviewed by the police in Bajina Basta, Serbia, concerning the attack on my village and my imprisonment." Now, do you recall that interview?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask if the witness can be shown a copy of that -- a note of that interview, and there are copies for the Court. And the ERN is RR321946 in the original. And the court officer in Belgrade has a copy of that document. That note, again, for the record, is an interview by the Republika Srpska, Minister of Internal Affairs, public security station, dated 5th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that note in front of you, Ms. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly, that statement correctly records your personal details at the time, doesn't it? Your parents' names, Nikola and Zivana, where you lived. First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read a part of that note, and I refer you to the first four sentences of the second paragraph, and it reads: "When our village was attacked on January 16, 1993, I was in the house of my grandmother. When we heard shots, Grandmother and I ran out of the house and started running away. Somewhere around Milenko's house we split, and I ran to Drago's bakery where I spent the night." Now, that's the same as what you've told us today, isn't it, Drago's bakery and leaving your grandmother at Milenko's house.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. We separated on the way, near his barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. But the gist of it is what you've told us today. I'm going to read another section of that note, further down in the same paragraph: "When we arrived to the prison in Srebrenica, I saw that there were also Stojanka from Vizovici, Milena and Stana Mitrovic, Milenija, Milka from Kusic, Andja from Novo Selo, who had already been in prison for 4 to 5 months; Danica from Kusic, and some Dostana with her daughter-in-law and two children, all of them from Bjelovac. I also saw some Jelka and an older woman with grey hair. There were 15 women in that prison, and a young boy, Branko, from Zarkovici. As for men, I saw Mico, Ilija from Cosici, and Stanko from Kusic there." Now stopping there, it's right, isn't it, that at that time you remembered a great deal about the people who you saw from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your memory of events, then, was much fresher on the 5th of February than it is now, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, further down, you refer to some other people. "While I was in Srebrenica I met Fikret, a prison guard, and some Krdjo who drove a small blue truck. I also met cooks, Mirfeta, Zumra, and Jaca, as well as some Zele who either didn't have an arm or he was wounded in the right arm, because his right sleeve was always in the pocket or hanging. He is short and has long brown/black hair." Now, does that refresh your memory as to some of the people who you saw in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The fact is, isn't it, that when you gave this statement, you were asked to remember as many people as you possibly could, even if you could only give a first name or a nickname or some physical characteristic. And you mentioned everyone who you could possibly think of in connection with your detention; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please, Ms. Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you gave the statement, the people who were interviewing you were very keen, were they not, to get you to mention every person you could think of who you had seen in Srebrenica, even if you could only mention a first name or a nickname or a physical characteristic. And you told them every name you could think of.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, looking at the statement, that you never mentioned Naser Oric on that occasion, when you mentioned all these other names. And you can look at your statement if that would assist you. It's right, isn't it, that his name is no where there in that official note. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The reason his name isn't there, isn't it, is because you hadn't heard of Oric when you gave this interview. You heard his name afterwards, after your release, from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the Muslims who said I was to be exchanged. They said he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's look at your note again. The note also states the following: "I stayed in prison for two days, and then I went to sleep at some Behara's apartment." It's right, isn't it, that in fact you only stayed in the prison for two days and not one month as you've been telling us today. Could you please answer the question, Ms. Trifunovic? And remember, you're under oath.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question, then?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I was in the prison all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's look at the date on this document, and it's in two places, the 5th of February, 1993, you'll see in the top left-hand column, and it's repeated at the top: "On the 5th of February, 1993, we had an informative interview with Trifunovic, Svetlana, daughter of Nikola and Zivana." The fact is you were being interviewed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republika Srpska on the 5th of February, and not in prison, as you've told us today, isn't it? You can give us a truthful answer, Ms. Trifunovic. If you want to change your answer as to how long you spent in the prison, then now is the time to do it.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was imprisoned for a month, and I was in prison. I didn't go anywhere else from the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if you look at this note again, details are included there of Drago's bakery and the rough area where you left your grandmother, all of which you've agreed is what occurred. Why would police or the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska invent the fact that you were -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's not for this witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: She may have an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. And also, it's taking it for granted that this was invented. I'm going to take the witness in my hands for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, before -- so I don't forget, may this be made an exhibit, a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it will be, definitely, Mr. Jones. Ms. Trifunovic, do you remember being interviewed by someone from Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs on the 5th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on that occasion, did you make a statement? Did you accept to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was this statement put in writing, taken in writing as you were answering the questions that were being put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered the questions that were put to me by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But was there anyone, say, with a tape recorder or with a typewriter or whatever, or with a notebook taking down notes of what you were answering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no one there with a machine. They were just asking me questions without any machines or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
